hints: Look for a carbon with four different groups attached. Check the ring carbon bonded to $\text{OH}$ and the side chain and ask if any other carbon has four single bonds to four different groups.

Look for $\text{C=C}$ bonds where each carbon has two different groups and free rotation is restricted. Decide which double bonds are acyclic and can show E/Z isomerism and which are locked in the ring.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral carbon**
Think of a chiral centre as a carbon with four single bonds to four completely different groups. Scan molecule A. Most carbons are $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{C=C}$, so they cannot be chiral. The ring carbon joined to $\text{OH}$, to two different ring directions, and to the $\text{-CH=CH-}$ side chain has four different single-bonded groups. That is your only chiral centre, so circle it.

Spot the E/Z double bonds**
Geometrical isomerism needs a $\text{C=C}$ with restricted rotation where each carbon carries two different groups. The $\text{C=C}$ inside the six membered ring is locked cis by the ring and cannot show E/Z isomerism. The two $\text{C=C}$ bonds in the side chain each have two different groups on each carbon, so both can exist as E and Z forms. Draw a line through each of those two acyclic double bonds only.

Final answer: Circle the tertiary alcohol carbon in the ring, the $\text{C(OH)}$ bonded to the side chain, as the only chiral centre.
Draw a line through the two acyclic $\text{C=C}$ bonds in the side chain: $\text{-CH=CH-}$ and $\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)=C(Et)(CO}_2\text{H)}$.

hints: Scan the structure from left to right for oxygen containing groups. Distinguish $\text{C=O}$ in the ring from $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ at the end of the chain.
Look at the $\text{OH}$ bonded to a carbon with no hydrogen and at the $\text{C=C}$ bonds. Recall how to classify an alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary.
walkthrough:
Pick out the carbonyl groups**
You have two different $\text{C=O}$ groups. In the six membered ring the $\text{C=O}$ is bonded to two carbons, that is a ketone. At the end of the side chain the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group is a carboxylic acid.

Pick out the alcohol and alkene**
The $\text{-OH}$ is attached to a carbon joined to three other carbons, so it is a tertiary alcohol. The $\text{C=C}$ bonds, in the ring and in the side chain, give the alkene functional group.
Final answer: ketone, (tertiary) alcohol, alkene, carboxylic acid

hints: Count electron domains at carbon. Triple bond means sp, double bond means sp2, only single bonds means sp3. Check if A contains any triple bonds.
walkthrough:
Count by bond type**
No $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ is present, so sp = 0. Each $\text{C=C}$ carbon and each $\text{C=O}$ carbon is $\text{sp}^2$. There are three $\text{C=C}$ bonds giving 6 carbons, plus one ketone carbon plus one carboxylic acid carbon, total $6 + 2 = 8$ $\text{sp}^2$ carbons. With 17 carbons in total, the remainder $17 - 8 = 9$ are single bonded only and are $\text{sp}^3$.
Final answer: sp carbons = 0, sp$^2$ carbons = 8, sp$^3$ carbons = 9

hints: Hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ cleaves every $\text{C=C}$ into carbonyl fragments. Focus on the side chain $\text{-CH=CH-C(CH}_3\text{)=C(Et)(CO}_2\text{H)}$ which must be cut at two places.

Use the given formulae $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$ and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$ to check fragment size. A $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}$ end becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ and a $\text{C(Et)(CO}_2\text{H)}$ end becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO-}$ attached to the retained $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
See where the molecule is cut**
Hot concentrated manganate(VII) is vigorous oxidation. It breaks each $\text{C=C}$ completely. The large ring fragment becomes X. The side chain is chopped at the two acyclic double bonds: $\text{-CH=CH-}$ and $\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)=C(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)(CO}_2\text{H)}$. Think of each double bond carbon becoming a $\text{C=O}$ carbon.

Build the two small fragments**
Cleavage of $\text{HO}_2\text{C-C(CH}_3\text{)=C(Et)(CO}_2\text{H)}$, formed after the first cleavage and further oxidation, gives two keto-acids. The left $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}$ side gives $\text{CH}_3\text{-C(=O)-CO}_2\text{H}$, which is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$, compound Y. The right $\text{C(Et)(CO}_2\text{H)}$ side gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-CO}_2\text{H}$, which is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$, compound Z. Both retain a ketone plus a carboxylic acid group.

Final answer: Y is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$, 2-oxopropanoic acid.
Z is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$, 2-oxobutanoic acid shown as 2-oxopentanoic acid in scheme counting, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$.

hints: Rank J, K and L by polarity. Compare number of $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups capable of hydrogen bonding with a simple ketone.
walkthrough:
Match polarity to distance travelled**
Spot 1 is highest, nearest the solvent front, so it interacted least with the polar stationary phase. That must be the least polar compound L, pentan-3-one, a ketone with no $\text{O-H}$. Spot 3 is lowest, held most strongly, so it is the most polar compound K, ethanedioic acid with two $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups. The middle spot 2 is the intermediate polarity keto-acid J.
Final answer: J $\text{CH}_3\text{COCO}_2\text{H}$ is spot 2, K $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ is spot 3, L $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is spot 1.

hints: Recall the phases: polar silica stationary phase, non-polar mobile phase. Ask which type of compound sticks to the polar plate and which dissolves better in the non-polar solvent.
walkthrough:
Link polarity to retention**
Picture the plate as polar silica that can hydrogen bond. A very polar acid like K sticks tightly by hydrogen bonding and dipole interactions, so the non-polar solvent cannot drag it far. A less polar ketone like L sticks only weakly, stays more in the mobile phase, and is carried high up the plate. So distance travelled decreases as polarity and strength of attraction to the stationary phase increase.

Final answer: The more polar the compound, the stronger the attractive forces to the polar stationary phase, so the less it moves. Less polar compounds have weaker attraction to the stationary phase and move further with the non-polar mobile phase.

hints: Remember $R_f$ compares two distances measured from the baseline: how far the spot moved versus how far the solvent moved.
walkthrough:
Define the ratio**
$R_f$ tells you how far a compound travelled relative to the solvent. Measure from the baseline (the mixture line) to the centre of the spot, divide by the distance from the baseline to the solvent front. A value near 1 means little retention, a value near 0 means strong retention.
Final answer: $R_f$ is the retardation factor or retention factor = distance moved by compound from baseline / distance travelled by solvent front from baseline.
